name: Kwanzaa
desc: Kwanzaa is an annual celebration of African-American culture held from 26 December to 1 January, culminating in a communal feast called Karamu, usually on the sixth day. The activist Maulana Karenga created it in 1966, in the aftermath of the Watts riots, drawing on his research into African harvest festival traditions; according to Karenga, the name derives from the Swahili phrase matunda ya kwanza, "first fruits". Each of its seven days is dedicated to one of the seven principles, the Nguzo Saba, and ceremonies include a candle-lighting ritual. Karenga at first meant it as an alternative to Christmas, but many African Americans who celebrate it also observe Christmas.

name: Boxing Day
desc: Boxing Day is a holiday celebrated on 26 December, the day after Christmas Day, which originated in the United Kingdom and is kept in several Commonwealth nations. It was once a day for giving gifts to those in need and usually coincides with the Christian festival of Saint Stephen's Day. The origin of the name is not definitive: it may refer to the alms boxes placed in churches, and in Britain tradesmen collected "Christmas boxes" of money or presents after Christmas, a custom mentioned in Samuel Pepys's diary in 1663. The Oxford English Dictionary gives the earliest attestation from Britain in 1743. In the United Kingdom outside Scotland, 26 December has been a bank holiday since 1871.

name: Chinese New Year
desc: Chinese New Year, also known as the Spring Festival, marks the beginning of a new year on the traditional lunisolar Chinese calendar, on the new moon that falls between 21 January and 20 February. The festival runs from New Year's Eve, when families gather for the reunion dinner, to the Lantern Festival on the 15th day of the year. Records of the first celebration can be traced to the Warring States period (475–221 BCE). Houses are cleaned, doors are decorated with red couplets, firecrackers are lit and money is given in red envelopes. It has influenced other new year celebrations, among them the Tết of Vietnam, the Seollal of Korea and the Losar of Tibet.

name: Ōmisoka
desc: Ōmisoka is the traditional Japanese celebration of the last day of the year. It was held on the final day of the 12th lunar month until Japan switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1873, when it was set as 31 December. Traditionally, house cleaning, the repaying of debts, purification and bathing were completed so that the new year could start fresh. About an hour before the New Year, people often eat a bowl of toshikoshi soba or udon, long noodles associated with crossing over from one year to the next. At midnight many visit a shrine or temple, and most Buddhist temples strike a large bell once for each of the 108 earthly temptations believed to cause human suffering.

name: Maslenitsa
desc: Maslenitsa is an Eastern Slavic religious and folk holiday celebrated during the last week before Great Lent, the eighth week before Eastern Orthodox Pascha. It has retained elements of Slavic mythology in its ritual and, according to archaeological evidence from the 2nd century CE, may be the oldest surviving Slavic holiday. Russians bake blini, and a straw effigy, Lady Maslenitsa, is paraded and then burned in a bonfire on Forgiveness Sunday, when relatives and friends ask each other for forgiveness. Large public celebrations became less common after the Russian Revolution in 1917 and under Soviet state atheism; since 2002 Moscow has staged a yearly festival next to the Red Square.

name: Candlemas
aka: Feast of the Presentation of Jesus Christ
Feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary
desc: Candlemas is a Christian feast day, kept on 2 February, that commemorates the presentation of Jesus at the Temple by Joseph and Mary, as told in the Gospel of Luke. It falls on what is traditionally the 40th day and the conclusion of the Christmas–Epiphany season. One of the oldest feasts of the church, it was recorded by the pilgrim Egeria as celebrated in Jerusalem in the 380s, and it was introduced to Rome and other places from the mid-7th century. Many Christians take candles to church to be blessed and use them for the rest of the year as a symbol of Jesus Christ, the "Light of the World". A German saying about a hedgehog's shadow on Candlemas was the origin of Groundhog Day.

name: Thanksgiving
desc: Thanksgiving is a national holiday celebrated on various dates in October and November in the United States, Canada, Saint Lucia and Liberia. It began as a day of giving thanks for the harvest, and its history in North America is rooted in English traditions of days of thanksgiving dating from the Protestant Reformation. A yearly thanksgiving is first documented in 1619 at Berkeley Hundred in Virginia; the 1621 harvest festival of Plymouth Colony, which the Wampanoag joined, was largely forgotten for hundreds of years and was termed "the first Thanksgiving" only in 1841. Abraham Lincoln made it a national holiday in 1863, and in 1941 Congress fixed it on the fourth Thursday in November.

name: Day of the Dead
desc: The Day of the Dead is a holiday traditionally celebrated on 1 and 2 November, widely observed in Mexico and among people of Mexican heritage elsewhere, in which family and friends gather to remember those who have died. Families build home altars called ofrendas with the favourite foods and beverages of the departed, and visit graves with calaveras and marigold flowers. Mexican academics are divided on whether it has indigenous pre-Hispanic roots or is a Spanish tradition recast in the 20th century, under the presidency of Lázaro Cárdenas, to encourage Mexican nationalism. In 2008 UNESCO added it to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

name: Guy Fawkes Night
desc: Guy Fawkes Night is an annual commemoration observed on 5 November, primarily in Great Britain, with bonfires and fireworks displays. It began in 1605, when Guy Fawkes, a member of the Gunpowder Plot, was arrested while guarding explosives placed beneath the House of Lords, and people lit bonfires around London to celebrate the survival of King James I. The Observance of 5th November Act 1605 mandated an annual public day of thanksgiving, and as Gunpowder Treason Day it became a focus for anti-Catholic sentiment, with effigies of the Pope burnt. Towards the end of the 18th century children began begging for money with effigies of Guy Fawkes. The Act was repealed in 1859.

name: Gunpowder Plot
desc: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was an unsuccessful attempt by a group of English Catholics, led by Robert Catesby, to kill King James VI of Scotland and I of England. The plan was to blow up the House of Lords on 5 November 1605, as the prelude to a revolt in the Midlands in which the king's nine-year-old daughter, Princess Elizabeth, was to be installed as head of state. After an anonymous letter of warning reached William Parker, 4th Baron Monteagle, a search on 4 November found Guy Fawkes guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder. Catesby was shot dead at Holbeche House; eight surviving conspirators, including Fawkes, were convicted in January 1606 and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered.

name: Diwali
desc: Diwali, or Dipavali, is the Hindu festival of lights. It is celebrated over five or six days between around mid-October and mid-November and is associated with the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil; Hindus connect it with the day Rama returned to his kingdom in Ayodhya after defeating the demon king Ravana, and with Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity. Jains mark the final liberation of Mahavira, and Sikhs the release of Guru Hargobind from a Mughal prison. The festival originated in the Indian subcontinent, likely as a combination of harvest festivals of ancient India. Celebrants light their homes and temples with diyas, oil lamps.

name: Christmas truce
desc: The Christmas truce was a series of widespread unofficial ceasefires, mainly along the Western Front of the First World War around Christmas in 1914. Roughly 100,000 British and German troops were involved. In some areas men from both sides went into no man's land on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day to exchange food and souvenirs; there were joint burial ceremonies, carols and games of football, while hostilities continued in other sectors. Pope Benedict XV had begged the warring governments for an official truce on 7 December 1914, which both sides refused. The following year only a few units arranged ceasefires, in part because of orders from commanders prohibiting truces.

name: Armistice Day
desc: Armistice Day is commemorated every year on 11 November to mark the armistice signed between the Allies of World War I and Germany at Compiègne, France, which took effect at 11:00 am on that day in 1918 and ended hostilities on the Western Front. The first official Armistice Day events were held in the grounds of Buckingham Palace on the morning of 11 November 1919 and included a two-minute silence for those who died in the war. Around the Second World War many countries changed the holiday's name and several widened it to all veterans: most Commonwealth states adopted the name Remembrance Day, and the United States changed it in 1954. The date is a national holiday in France.
